raw_response:
Well, I've been farming these 10 and a half mu for 50 years now, since I was 21. Me and my old lady — just the two of us, our kids moved to Shijiazhuang years ago and they don't farm. I'm 71, my back isn't what it used to be, and my knees hurt when the weather changes. We can't do the heavy work no more, so I have to hire help for harvest and plowing. That costs money, and at our age every yuan matters. My pension is only 158 yuan a month.

I got 6 mu in winter wheat that I planted last October. Used my own saved seed — no need to buy when you got good seed from the year before. For base fertilizer I put down about half a bag of compound fertilizer and maybe 15 jin of urea per mu. That money's already spent. Now it's April, the wheat is growing fast. I walked the field yesterday — looks a bit yellow in patches, needs a boost. I'm going to topdress with urea, about 15 jin per mu. I know fertilizer prices went up, urea is about 2.5 yuan per jin now, but I learned the hard way when I was young: skimp on fertilizer and you lose more in yield than you save in cost. Last year I put down about this much and got roughly 700 jin per mu. I'll irrigate two more times before harvest — once now when it's shooting up, once when the heads are filling — if the rain don't come. Pumping from the well costs about 20-25 yuan per mu each time, but wheat needs water. I'll spray once for bugs or mold if I see them; last year we had some aphids so I keep an eye out. For harvest in early June, I hire the combine — 60 yuan per mu. I can't cut wheat by hand at my age, and my wife can't either.

On the other 4 and a half mu, I'm planting spring maize in late April. I hire Old Zhang's tractor to plow — 50 yuan per mu. I buy hybrid seed from the supply shop, about 4 jin per mu. It's expensive, 30 yuan per mu, but hybrid seed gives better yield and maize seed don't breed true anyway, so you have to buy new every year. For fertilizer, I put compound fertilizer in the furrow when planting, about 50 jin per mu, and some urea too. Maize is hungry — it needs more feed than millet. I'll topdress with urea when it's knee-high, about another 20 jin per mu. Irrigate two times this summer, maybe three if it's real dry. Spray herbicide after planting — cheaper than weeding by hand, though me and my wife still walk the field and pull the big weeds. Harvest in late September, I'll hire people to help pick and shell. Expecting maybe 800 jin per mu if the weather is decent.

Then comes the hard part — mid-June, right after wheat harvest, I got to get the summer millet in on those same 6 mu. The window is tight, maybe 5-7 days. If it rains during harvest, I'm in trouble. I hire the combine for the wheat, then Old Zhang comes right after to rotary till. I don't plow deep — no time, and millet don't need it. I use mostly saved millet seed, maybe buy a little to top up, about 2 jin per mu. Millet is easy — it don't need much fertilizer. I put down about 40 jin of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and maybe 15 jin of urea. That's it. Millet can take dry weather better than maize, so I'll irrigate it once or twice, mostly to help it get started. Me and my wife do the weeding by hand — no money for herbicide on millet, and the rows are wide enough to walk through. Harvest in late September or early October, we cut it with sickles and thresh it. It's hard work but the machine can't do millet proper. Millet prices are good — last year I got 4.5 yuan per jin, better than maize. Yield won't be as high, maybe 500 jin per mu, but it's less water and less heavy lifting.

Why millet instead of maize on the 6 mu? I've done wheat-millet for over 30 years. My neighbor Old Wang switched to wheat-maize and his son helps with the machines and carrying. But me and my wife, we can't handle the heavy maize harvest on top of wheat in that busy week. Millet is lighter to thresh and carry, and it uses less water. With well irrigation getting expensive every year, millet makes sense for us old folks. Also, if maize prices drop or there's a drought, I still have the millet money. It's my insurance. I don't try to get rich — I just don't want to lose money.

Labor is tight. My wife and I can spread fertilizer, open water channels, pull weeds, but we can't lift heavy bags or run machines no more. This year I'll hire about 12 days of labor total — mostly for harvest, plowing, and that busy week in June. At 130 yuan per day, that's over 1,500 yuan just for hired hands. It hurts to pay it, but what can I do? My body won't let me do what I did at 40.

Money is always tight. I need about 4,000 yuan for inputs this year — fertilizer, seed, hired labor, pumping, pesticides. I try to keep 1,000 yuan aside for my wife's blood pressure medicine. So I watch every cost, but I know that not spending on fertilizer or irrigation costs me more at harvest. A bad year hurts worse than a good year helps. I'd rather put down a bit too much urea than too little and watch my yield drop. Slow and steady. I've seen too many bad years to get greedy.
